events.speaker: Helen
events.text: Thanks everyone. Today we need to agree on how we integrate the two engineering teams. We've got 40 people from Legacy Co and 18 from the acquired team. The plan is to fold the acquired team into our existing structure — same processes, same tools, same reporting lines.

events.speaker: David
events.text: That makes sense. We have mature processes here. It's easier if everyone works the same way.

events.speaker: Mark
events.text: Agreed. Our CI/CD pipeline and sprint cadence are well established. Onboarding the new team onto our systems is the logical move.

events.speaker: Helen
events.text: Good. So we standardise on our stack, our tools, our ways of working. Sophie, Priya — you'll need to start the transition plans for your teams.

intervention.question: Why are you so certain that bigger means better, and has anyone actually audited whether your 'mature processes' are producing outcomes worth replicating?
intervention.context: The room is defaulting to the oldest corporate integration habit: majority wins, absorb the minority, call it standardisation. Nobody has asked what the 18-person team was doing that made them worth acquiring in the first place — and whether your CI/CD pipeline and sprint cadence are the reason to buy them or the thing that will destroy the value you just paid for.

events.speaker: Sophie
events.text: I want to raise something before we finalise that. The acquired team has some pretty different ways of working that have produced strong results. Their deployment frequency is three times ours. Their incident rate is half.

events.speaker: Helen
events.text: That's a different context though. Smaller team, different product.

events.speaker: Mark
events.text: Our processes are designed for scale. What works for 18 people doesn't necessarily work for 40.

events.speaker: Priya
events.text: Some of our engineers are already nervous about this integration. A few of them joined specifically because of our engineering culture. If we ask them to abandon everything overnight—

events.speaker: Helen
events.text: Change is always uncomfortable. That's normal in a merger.

events.speaker: David
events.text: The sooner we standardise, the sooner we get to one culture. Dragging it out just prolongs the uncertainty.

intervention.question: Which specific engineers are flight risks, and does leadership actually know their names or are we just abstracting 'nervousness' into a category so no one has to make a hard call about retaining them?
intervention.context: The team is laundering a concrete retention crisis into a general change-management conversation. If two or three key engineers walk in month two because standardisation felt like erasure, the integration cost and timeline collapse — and the postmortem will show this moment as when the warning was audible and ignored.

events.speaker: Sophie
events.text: I'm not suggesting we drag it out. I'm suggesting we look at what's actually working before we decide what to standardise on.

events.speaker: Helen
events.text: We don't have time for a full audit. The board wants integration milestones by end of Q2.

intervention.question: What if the pressure to standardise fast is actually the thing that destroys the value you paid for in the first place?
intervention.context: Post-merger integration research consistently shows that speed-to-standardisation is inversely correlated with value retention when the acquired entity was bought for its culture or capabilities — not just its assets. The hospitality and professional services sectors offer particularly sharp precedents where aggressive cultural homogenisation triggered the precise talent exodus that collapsed the acquisition rationale within 18 months.

events.speaker: Mark
events.text: We could lose months trying to evaluate two sets of processes. Let's just pick one and move forward.

intervention.question: Who decided that standardisation means picking one culture's way of doing things and erasing the other, and why is that the only version of integration anyone in this room is imagining?
intervention.context: The team is trapped inside a false binary: audit everything slowly versus pick one side and bulldoze forward. Nobody is questioning whether 'one culture' is even the right destination — the radical alternative is building a third, deliberately designed operating model that cherry-picks the best of both and is built for where the merged entity is going, not where either company came from.

events.speaker: Priya
events.text: I'm worried we're going to lose some of our best engineers over this.

events.speaker: Helen
events.text: Retention is always a risk in mergers. HR will handle that.

events.speaker: David
events.text: We have a standard retention package ready.

events.speaker: Sophie
events.text: A retention package doesn't fix a cultural fit problem.

events.speaker: Helen
events.text: Look, we need to make a decision today. Are we aligned on standardising to our existing processes?

intervention.question: What specific evidence do we have that the acquired company's top talent actually wants to stay under our processes, or are we assuming the retention package buys us silence rather than commitment?
intervention.context: The team is treating retention as a financial transaction while actively avoiding the question of whether standardising processes will trigger the exact exodus it's designed to prevent. Discovering that key people left because of process imposition costs infinitely more post-close than honest due diligence on cultural incompatibility costs right now.

events.speaker: Mark
events.text: Yes.

events.speaker: David
events.text: Yes.

events.speaker: Priya
events.text: I... yes. But I want it noted that I have concerns.

events.speaker: Sophie
events.text: Same. Noted concerns.

events.speaker: Helen
events.text: Noted. Let's move to the migration timeline.
